note: 102 studies covering 2.8 million patients, only 45 percent used high evidence validation and only 14 percent shared data.
title: Artificial Intelligence in Surgery: A Systematic Review of Use and Validation
explain_beginner: The question, across the whole field of surgery, how much has AI actually been tested, and when a study claims its AI tool works, how solid is the proof behind that claim. Surgeons and hospitals cared because AI is being proposed for everything from predicting surgical complications before an operation to guiding instruments during one, but a technology being tried is not the same as a technology being properly proven, and they needed a sense of how much of the excitement was backed by strong evidence versus a single small study. Reviewing 102 studies covering nearly 2.8 million patients across specialties from orthopedics to cardiac surgery, the authors found the large majority of AI applications, just over half, were being used to predict a patient's risk before surgery rather than to guide the surgeon's hands during the operation itself, and only 45 percent of these studies met the review's bar for high quality validation. What it does not settle is whether the roughly 55 percent of studies with weaker validation are actually wrong, only that the evidence behind them is not yet strong enough to be confident either way, and the review also found only 14 percent of studies shared their underlying data publicly, which limits independent checking of the results.
explain_business: A hospital or surgical department evaluating an AI tool for pre-operative risk prediction, by far the most common use case in this review, should specifically ask whether that tool's validation falls into the roughly 45 percent with high quality evidence or the majority with weaker support, since this review found that split to be nearly even across the field as a whole. Because only 14 percent of the underlying studies shared their data, independently verifying a vendor's specific performance claim is often not possible using published literature alone, so contractual rights to run local validation testing become more important than usual in negotiations. Intra-operative, hands on guidance tools remain a small slice of the field, just 5 percent of applications here, meaning a buyer looking for that specific capability should expect a much thinner evidence base than for pre-operative risk tools. The review does not address regulatory clearance status directly, so procurement teams still need to check FDA or equivalent approval separately from the validation quality question it raises. This is most useful right now during vendor comparison, as a prompt to ask pointed questions rather than accept a headline accuracy number at face value.
explain_practitioner: Method, a systematic review of 102 studies covering 2,837,211 patients in total, with an aggregate dataset size of 18,137,987 across the included studies, spanning surgical specialties including orthopedics and spine, general surgery, anesthesiology, urology and gynecology, plastic surgery, ophthalmology, otolaryngology, and cardiac and thoracic surgery. By application, 51 percent targeted risk prediction or reduction, 17 percent outcome prediction, 13 percent prognosis assessment, 11 percent pre-operative evaluation and planning, and 5 percent intra-operative technique assistance, with 62 percent of applications situated in the pre-operative period, 31 percent involving medical imaging, and 26 percent tied to cancer care. The review's central metric is validation quality rather than head to head algorithm performance, finding only 45 percent of studies achieved high evidence validation while 55 percent showed moderate evidence or lower, and only 16 percent applied methods the authors considered adequate for real world application. The authors report a direct limitation, only 14 percent of studies made their datasets publicly available, limiting reproducibility, and 44 percent of the original studies' own authors explicitly acknowledged validation weaknesses, meaning the evidence gap identified here is one the primary researchers largely recognized themselves.
